newsitem.title: USA: U.S. economy even stronger in 1st quarter but slowing.
newsitem.headline: U.S. economy even stronger in 1st quarter but slowing.

text.p: Economic growth was even stronger than estimated in the first quarter, the government said Friday, though growth has slowed enough since then that the Federal Reserve is unlikely to raise interest rates next week.

The economy grew at a 5.9 percent annual rate in the quarter, up from the 5.8 percent rate previously estimated, helped by a better performance in international trade, the Commerce Department said in its final revision of Gross Domestic Product, the broadest measure of the nation's economy.
It was the strongest quarter in more than nine years, since growth of 6 percent in the fourth quarter of 1987.

But analysts said the exceptionally strong growth, aided by warm weather that boosted home building and other industries across much of the country, has tapered off since as consumers pulled back on spending.

"It was a strong quarter, too hot for comfort, but it apparently has been followed by a much slower second quarter," said Robert Dederick at Northern Trust Co. in Chicago. He estimated growth of about 2 percent in the current quarter.

That will make it easier for Fed policy-makers who meet on Tuesday and Wednesday to forego raising rates again. The central bank raised short-term rates in March, the first increase in more than two years, in a bid to ward off inflation. But they held rates steady last month.
As in the earlier estimates, there were scant signs of a pickup in inflation in Friday's report despite the economy's strength, which can fuel increases in prices and wages.
The Fed policy-makers "can sit back and relax and make Fourth of July plans," Dederick said. "It would be hard for them to act in the face of sensational inflation numbers."
Two inflation measures in the report showed prices rising at a 2.2 percent rate or a 2.7 percent rate, depending on the method used, but in either case the increases were mild.

A better trade picture helped boost growth in the quarter, more than offsetting slightly lower estimates of production and consumer spending, the department said. It estimated the trade figures a month ago but had final data for Friday's report.

Economist Gary Thayer at A.G. Edwards and Sons in St. Louis noted that strong business profits augured well for the economy, which has grown steadily since the last recession ended in spring 1991, since they point to continued business investment.

Thayer said that overall growth slowed to about a 2 percent rate in the current quarter but would probably accelerate because job growth is strong and that, along with stock market gains, has made consumers more confident.
A separate report showed consumer confidence rose in June. The University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index rose to 104.5 from 103.2 in May, according to people who saw the report.

The department's revised figures showed that imports grew at a $44.7 billion rate in the first quarter compared with the $51.6 billion estimated a month ago. That lowered the trade deficit and subtracted less from the dollar value of GDP.

The improved trade performance more than offset weaker production for inventories, which grew at $48.6 billion rate, down from the $51.4 billion estimated a month ago, and consumer spending, which rose at a $65.5 billion rate instead of $66.2 billion.
Business profits grew at an annual rate of $42.4 billion in the first quarter to $712.5 billion.
